title: Cochinita Pibil
subtitle: Yucatecan slow-roasted achiote pork
excerpt: Cochinita pibil is a Yucatecan dish of pork marinated in achiote paste and sour citrus juice, then slow-roasted until falling apart. It is vivid brick-red in colour, deeply savoury and slightly tangy. Serve it shredded into warm corn tortillas.
sourceNotes: Cochinita pibil originates in the Yucatan Peninsula and takes its name from the Mayan word 'pib', meaning to cook underground. Traditionally the pork was wrapped in banana leaves and slow-cooked in a pit oven dug into the earth.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked shredded pork in its cooking juices for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the pork overnight for the best colour and flavour.

glossaryTerms.definition: A paste or powder made from annatto seeds, used throughout Latin America for its vivid brick-red colour and mild earthy flavour. It is the key ingredient in cochinita pibil.

content.text: This recipe serves 6 and takes 3 hours in the oven plus a short marinade. The longer you marinate the pork, the deeper the colour and flavour, so overnight in the fridge is worth the planning.

The citrus mix for the marinade is sour orange juice, which is traditional in Yucatan. Outside of Mexico, a combination of lime juice and orange juice gives the right balance of sharp and sweet. Use 3 limes and 2 oranges squeezed together.
Make the marinade. Put the achiote paste, lime juice, juice of 2 oranges and the garlic cloves into a blender. Blend until smooth. The colour should be a vivid orange-red.

Score the pork shoulder all over with a sharp knife, making cuts about 2 cm deep. This allows the marinade to penetrate the meat. Place the pork in a large bowl or zip-lock bag and pour over the marinade, turning to coat completely. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight.

Heat the oven to 160°C. Scatter the sliced onion over the base of a roasting tin. Lift the pork out of its marinade and sit it on top of the onions. Pour any remaining marinade over the top. Cover the tin tightly with two layers of foil so no steam can escape.
Roast for 3 hours without lifting the foil. The pork is ready when it pulls apart with no resistance. If the joint is bone-in, the bone should slide out cleanly.

Lift the pork onto a board. Shred it thoroughly using two forks, discarding any large chunks of fat and the bone. Return the shredded pork to the roasting tin and stir it through the cooking juices and softened onions.

Warm the corn tortillas directly over a gas flame for 30 seconds per side, or in a dry frying pan. Pile the shredded pork onto the tortillas and serve with pickled red onions and habanero salsa if you have them.

attrs.symptom: The pork is still firm after 3 hours.
attrs.cause: The foil seal was not tight enough and steam escaped, reducing the braising effect.
attrs.fix: Reseal with fresh foil and return to the oven for another 30 to 45 minutes, checking again.

attrs.symptom: The marinade looks pale rather than brick-red.
attrs.cause: Some brands of achiote paste vary in intensity. The colour fades further with dilution.
attrs.fix: Add another 20 g of achiote paste and blend again. A good red is worth chasing as it affects the final look of the dish.

attrs.symptom: The meat is dry after shredding.
attrs.cause: The foil was lifted during cooking, or the marinade was not enough to create sufficient braising liquid.
attrs.fix: Stir in a splash of water or orange juice with the shredded meat in the tin. Place back in the oven for 10 minutes uncovered to let the liquid absorb.
